practice.context: A student is planning an information report about local wetlands. Which research plan best supports accurate writing?
practice.correct: Gather facts from more than one reliable source, record where each fact came from, then group related notes before drafting.
distractors: Copy the first webpage found.
Use only memory and add sources later if needed.
Collect many facts without recording where they came from.
practice.rationale: Effective planning gathers relevant information from reliable sources and organises it before drafting.
practice.hint: Record sources while researching and sort notes by the ideas they support.

practice.context: A draft about recycling has one paragraph mixing collection days, what plastics are accepted and why recycling matters. What is the best revision?
practice.correct: Group sentences into focused paragraphs, such as collection details, accepted materials and reasons recycling matters.
distractors: Keep all ideas in one paragraph because they share a broad topic.
Put each sentence in a separate paragraph.
Move the heading to the end and change nothing else.
practice.rationale: Paragraphs help sequence and group related ideas so readers can follow the text’s structure.
practice.hint: Give each paragraph a clear focus that supports the text’s purpose.

practice.context: Which sentence uses the most precise vocabulary for an information text about erosion?
practice.correct: “Fast-moving water can carry loosened soil downstream.”
distractors: “Water does stuff to dirt.”
“The water is really, really strong and bad.”
“Things move somewhere.”
practice.rationale: Precise, topic-appropriate vocabulary communicates information accurately and efficiently.
practice.hint: Replace vague words with exact nouns, verbs and technical terms where useful.

practice.context: A story draft says, “The dog ran. The gate was open.” Which revision uses grammar to connect the ideas clearly?
practice.correct: “Because the gate was open, the dog ran into the lane.”
distractors: “The dog the gate open ran.”
“Running open gate dog.”
“The gate was open. Because.”
practice.rationale: A complex sentence can show a meaningful relationship such as cause, time or condition between ideas.
practice.hint: Choose a clause link that expresses the intended relationship clearly.

practice.context: A report shifts from “The platypus lives in freshwater habitats” to “It hunted at night yesterday” without a reason. What should the writer edit?
practice.correct: Choose a tense that suits the report’s purpose and keep it consistent unless the time reference genuinely changes.
distractors: Use a different tense in every sentence for variety.
Remove all verbs.
Change all nouns into adjectives.
practice.rationale: Appropriate and consistent tense helps readers understand when events or facts apply.
practice.hint: Check whether tense changes are purposeful rather than accidental.

practice.context: A paragraph repeats “The solar oven gets hot. The solar oven cooks food. The solar oven uses sunlight.” Which revision improves cohesion?
practice.correct: “The solar oven uses sunlight to become hot enough to cook food.”
distractors: “The solar oven. Hot. Food. Sunlight.”
“It it it gets hot and it.”
“The solar oven uses sunlight. Bananas are yellow.”
practice.rationale: Editing can combine related ideas, reduce unnecessary repetition and make connections clearer.
practice.hint: Use pronouns, connectives and sentence combining only when they make relationships clearer.

test.context: A student has notes from a library book and a government webpage about bushfire preparation. What is the best next step before drafting?
test.correct: Compare the information, keep relevant points, record both sources and organise notes under planned sections.
distractors: Merge sentences by copying them word for word.
Use whichever source has more pictures.
Delete source details once notes are taken.
test.rationale: Writers integrate researched information by selecting, organising and attributing useful evidence.
test.hint: Plan how each source contributes rather than copying source wording.

test.context: A persuasive text has reasons scattered randomly before the position is stated. Which revision most improves structure?
test.correct: State the position clearly, group related reasons into paragraphs and finish with a conclusion suited to the audience.
distractors: Put every sentence in alphabetical order.
Add more adjectives without changing organisation.
Move the title to the bottom.
test.rationale: Text structure should help the audience follow the purpose and progression of ideas.
test.hint: Organise ideas in a sequence that supports the text’s purpose.

test.context: Which revision best improves the sentence “The animal went quickly into its home” in a report about wombats?
distractors: “The thing went somewhere fast.”
“The wombat was very, very going.”
“Home animal quickly.”
test.rationale: Specific nouns and verbs make information more precise and efficient.
test.hint: Choose exact vocabulary that fits the topic and meaning.

test.context: A draft says, “When the rain stopped. We returned to the oval.” Which edit creates a correct complex sentence?
test.correct: “When the rain stopped, we returned to the oval.”
distractors: “When the rain stopped we.”
“The rain stopped because.”
“Returned to the oval when.”
test.rationale: The dependent clause needs an independent clause to form a complete complex sentence.
test.hint: Check that a dependent clause is attached to a complete independent clause.
